with_sayso.hash-lookup:
People call hash map lookup O(1) because hashing the key selects a bucket and reading that array slot takes constant time. When the hash spreads keys evenly and the load factor (entries divided by buckets) stays within a fixed bound, the number of other keys you have to check stays constant on average. Expected lookup time therefore stays independent of how many entries the map holds.

A normal collision is already part of that average. The O(1) description stops holding when the extra work grows with the map.

If many keys share one bucket, a weak hash or a set of keys built to collide makes lookup walk a chain or a probe run that can reach O(n). If the table never grows, the load factor rises with the entry count, and the expected length of that walk rises with it. If the key is long, hashing it and comparing it cost time proportional to the key. On a table that no longer fits in cache, the number of probes can stay bounded while each probe is no longer a cheap read. Where a long chain is stored as a tree, the worst case is O(log n).
with_sayso.load-note-review:
A caller receives the text of the file `open` reads, or the exception `open` or `read` raises.

**The path can leave that user's directory.** `user_id` and `name` are copied into `/notes/{user_id}/{name}` with no check. `open` resolves `..` and follows symlinks, so those inputs can name a file outside `/notes/{user_id}/`. The caller receives that file's contents. If that path cannot be read, the caller receives the exception instead. Read the file only when its resolved path is still inside `/notes/{user_id}`.

**The cache key drops `user_id`.** A successful call stores the text at `cache[name]`. A later call with the same `name` and a different `user_id` replaces that entry, so a later reader of `cache[name]` receives the other user's text. The caller of `load_note` receives the text from its own read. Key the cache by `user_id` and `name`.

If `open` or `read` raises, the assignment is skipped, so the existing `cache[name]` entry stays. A later reader of that key still receives the previous text.

**The decoded text follows the process locale.** `open` uses text mode and sets no encoding, so it decodes with the locale encoding and rewrites every newline as `\n`. The caller receives that string. Bytes that cannot be decoded raise `UnicodeDecodeError`. Pass the encoding the notes are stored in. Pass `newline=""` as well when the caller needs the file's original newline characters. The snippet does not name the encoding.

The snippet leaves two points open. It uses `cache` without binding it, so a missing binding raises `NameError` after the read and the caller receives no text. It also does not show overlapping calls. The read and the cache assignment are separate steps, so an overlapping call can store a newer read and then lose it when the earlier call assigns.

without_sayso.hash-lookup:
Hash map lookup is called O(1) because a hash function turns the key into a bucket index in one shot, and a table that resizes to keep its load factor bounded has only a constant number of keys in that bucket on average. You hash, jump to the bucket, and check a handful of entries — the work does not grow with how many keys are stored.

That stops being true in the worst case. If many keys land in the same bucket, a chain becomes a linear scan, so lookup is O(n). A predictable hash makes this easy to force. It also fails when the hash of the key itself is not constant-time (a long string costs work proportional to its length), or when the table never resizes and buckets keep getting longer. A single insert that triggers a resize is O(n) too; the O(1) claim is about the expected cost of a lookup while the load factor stays bounded, not every individual operation.
without_sayso.load-note-review:
The function has three result-changing bugs:

- The cache key is only `name`, so one user’s note overwrites another’s when the names match. A later lookup of `cache[name]` returns the wrong user’s text.
- `user_id` and `name` are inserted into the path with no checks. `..` or extra separators make `open` read a different file, so the caller gets that file’s contents or an unexpected error.
- `open(path)` uses the locale encoding. The same file can come back as different text, or the call can raise `UnicodeDecodeError`, depending on the process locale.
